extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent examiners, and law students (U.S. patent practice)
extracted.subtask_description: A compilation of U.S. patent law principles and procedural/substantive holdings (case-based rules) governing prosecution, abandonment, claims, assignment, infringement, damages, construction, disclaimers, designs, and related topics. Useful for practitioners and students applying case precedent to patent matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner duty to disclose basis
rubrics_metrics.description: That an examiner must give the applicant all the information on which he bases his judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ex parte Pastor (1887). Duty to disclose prior art/reasons forming the basis of an adverse action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver of cross-reference requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: That an examiner may waive his requirement for cross-references between pending applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ex parte Donovan (1888). PTO discretion to waive cross-reference requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisional applications treated re: prior use
rubrics_metrics.description: That divisional applications are treated as the same proceeding with reference to prior use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Frankfort Whiskey Process Co. v. Mill Creek Distilling Co. (1889). Continuity for prior use purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unavoidable delay does not abandon
rubrics_metrics.description: That unavoidable delay in prosecuting an application does not abandon it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ligowski Clay Pigeon Co. v. American Clay Bird Co. (1888). Excusable delays can avoid abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension request cannot exceed two years
rubrics_metrics.description: That an application cannot be suspended at the request of the applicant for more than two years without abandoning it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ex parte Norton (1888). Applicant-requested suspensions limited to preserve application status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Last action must be regular and legal
rubrics_metrics.description: That the 'last action' of the Patent Office must be some regular and legal action for the preservation or obtaining of the right, not an irregular and illegal step taken by the applicant and a refusal of the Office to recognize it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Kirk v. Commissioner (1886). The final proper act must be by the Office to preserve rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-faith minor amendments save from abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: That amendments filed in good faith but not important in character are such prosecution of the application as saves it from abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ex parte Todd (1889). Minor, good-faith amendments can preserve application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal amendment may be accepted conditionally
rubrics_metrics.description: That an informal amendment may be received by the Office to save the application from abandonment, upon condition that the amendment be subsequently made to comply with the rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ex parte Sullivan (1888). Office may accept informal filings with later formalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments not changing status don't prevent abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: That amendments not removing objections nor changing the status of the application in the Office are not such prosecution as prevents its abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ex parte Edison (1888). Mere filings that don't address objections/status won't avoid abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second original can be filed after two-year neglect
rubrics_metrics.description: That a second original application for the same invention can be filed after the first is abandoned by two years' neglect to renew after forfeiture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ex parte Bamitz (1888). Refiling options after abandonment by neglect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandoned application not a bar to subsequent patent
rubrics_metrics.description: That an abandoned application is no bar to a subsequent patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Beach v. Fowler (1889). Abandonment eliminates blocking effect of prior application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandoned or rejected application not citable as reference
rubrics_metrics.description: That an abandoned or rejected application cannot be cited as a reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Webster v. Sanford (1888). PTO/courts may not treat abandoned/rejected apps as anticipatory references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copies of abandoned cases furnished on application; inspection denied
rubrics_metrics.description: That copies of abandoned cases in the Patent Office must be furnished on application if needed for purposes of evidence, but a motion to inspect such cases generally will be denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ex parte Fowler (1889); United States v. Hall (1889). Paper copies may be provided; in-person inspection discouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney may seek mandamus for copies of abandoned apps
rubrics_metrics.description: That an attorney at law may obtain a mandamus against the Commissioner in his own name to procure copies of abandoned applications from the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: United States v. Hall (1889). Judicial remedy to compel production of files.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity requires same invention
rubrics_metrics.description: That applications are not continuous unless they cover the same invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Green v. Hall (1889). Continuation/continuity limited to identical invention subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: New application at PTO suggestion treated as continuation
rubrics_metrics.description: That a new application filed at the suggestion of the Patent Office is a continuation of the old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: International Tooth Crown Co. v. Richmond (1887). PTO-directed refilings may be treated as continuations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executor-filed application treated as continuation
rubrics_metrics.description: That a new application filed by the executor of a deceased applicant is a continuation of the former application and has the same status in the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ex parte Smith (1888). Continuation status extends to executor filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: No right to forfeit and renew at will
rubrics_metrics.description: That an applicant has no right to forfeit an application and file a renewal at his option.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ex parte Manny (1888). Applicant can't deliberately forfeit to restart prosecution arbitrarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowed applications must be issued absent defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: That an allowed application cannot be withheld when neither reference, publication, public use, nor interference can be urged against it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ex parte Atwood (1888). PTO should not withhold an allowed application without valid grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaust administrative appeals before bill in equity
rubrics_metrics.description: That in an ex parte case in the Patent Office the remedies by appeal must be exhausted before a bill in equity to obtain the patent can be filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Kirk v. Commissioner (1886). Administrative remedies are prerequisite to equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary should not be party to bill for patent
rubrics_metrics.description: That the Secretary should not be made a party to a bill to obtain a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Kirk v. Commissioner (1886). Procedural guidance on proper parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court may decide patentability on appeal from equity decree
rubrics_metrics.description: That on an appeal from a decree in equity granting a patent to one of two rival inventors on the sole ground of his priority, the defeated party may raise the question of the patentability of the invention and the Supreme Court may decide it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Hill v. Wooster (1890). Higher court may examine patentability even where priority was basis of decree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art patentable like machine or composition
rubrics_metrics.description: That an art is as truly the subject of a patent as a machine or composition of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: The Telephone Cases (1888). Process or art patentability equal to other categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processes producing electrical current change patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: That a process consisting in the production and use of a change in the condition of an electrical current is patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: The Telephone Cases (1888). Patentable subject matter can include electrical processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art new if final step is new
rubrics_metrics.description: That an art is new if the final step is new, though the other steps and the apparatus are old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Frankfort Whiskey Process Co. v. Mill Creek Distilling Co. (1889). Novel final step can render whole process new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of step can produce new art
rubrics_metrics.description: That a new art may be produced by omitting one of the steps regarded as necessary in an old one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Lawther v. Hamilton (1888). Novel simplification by omission can be patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process mere function of machine not separately patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: That a process which is the mere function of a machine is not separately patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ex parte Simmonds (1888). Processes that are inseparable from a machine may not be distinct inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical process separately patentable if performable by other apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: That a mechanical process capable of being performed by other apparatus than the machine devised by its inventor for the purpose is separately patentable, unless dedicated to the public by the use of the machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ex parte Young (1888). Process vs. machine distinction depends on generality and dedication to public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title vests in assignee of record on issue
rubrics_metrics.description: That the title to the patent, to whomsoever granted, vests on its issue in the ultimate assignee of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Consolidated Electric Light Co. v. McKeesport Light Co. (1888). Assignment effects upon issuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single claim may be assigned
rubrics_metrics.description: That a single claim of a patent may be assigned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Pope Mfg. Co. v. Gormully & Jeffrey Mfg. Co. (1888). Assignability of portions of patent rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of all interest for term can transfer entire title
rubrics_metrics.description: That an assignment of all the patentee's interest in the patent for the whole term, with all re-issues, renewals, and extensions, for one fourth of the future proceeds, transfers the entire title to the assignee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Rude v. Westcott (1889). Substantive effect of broad assignment grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer for royalties leaves interest in transferor
rubrics_metrics.description: That the transfer of an exclusive right to make, use, and sell, upon the payment of certain royalties, leaves an interest in the transferor and is not an absolute assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Clement Mfg. Co. v. Upson & Hall Co. (1889). Distinction between license and assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transferee of undivided interest limited in prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: That the transferee of an undivided interest in the invention for a certain part of the United States is not an assignee, and cannot join in prosecuting an application for a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ex parte Funston (1889). Geographic-slice transfers do not equate to full assignment for prosecution rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney assignments must be in principal's name and sealed
rubrics_metrics.description: That an assignment made by attorney must be executed in the name of the principal, and sealed with his seal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Machesney v. Brown (1886). Formalities required for attorney-executed assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of rights of action must be clearly expressed
rubrics_metrics.description: That an assignment of rights of action must be clearly expressed, and if procured pending suit by an assignee of the patent cannot be set up by supplemental bill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Emerson v. Hubbard (1888). Clarity required to effect transfer of enforcement rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent attorneys not expected to be learned lawyers
rubrics_metrics.description: That patent attorneys and solicitors are not expected to be learned lawyers, and indulgence should be shown to applicants on that account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Osgood v. Badger (1888). Practical leniency toward practitioners' legal breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor's attorney recognized until assignee asserts rights
rubrics_metrics.description: That the attorney of the inventor will be recognized by the Patent Office until the assignee asserts his rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ex parte Baker (1889). Representation recognized until assignee intervenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design caveat not allowable if design incomplete
rubrics_metrics.description: That as a design cannot be incomplete no caveat for it is allowable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ex parte Carty (1888). Caveat rules differ for designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate notice to caveator on apparent conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: That when an application apparently conflicts with a pending caveat notice should be sent at once to the caveator without waiting to determine the patentability of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ex parte Ward (1889). Prompt procedural protections for caveators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveator not bound to file application after notice
rubrics_metrics.description: That a caveator after notice is not bound to file any application, nor can he excuse himself for lack of diligence in filing it, nor will an applicant be delayed to wait for an application from a caveator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ex parte Ward (1889); Elges v. Miller (1889). Caveat confers limited rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matter not claimed not covered by patent
rubrics_metrics.description: That matter not claimed is not covered by the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Dickinson v. Parker (1889); Van Camp v. Maryland Pavement Co. (1888). Claim scope controls coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee bound by his claim
rubrics_metrics.description: That the patentee is bound by his claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Electrical Accumulator Co. v. Julien Electric Co. (1889). Claims define patentee's rights and limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims should leave details to Description
rubrics_metrics.description: That the Claim should leave it to the Description to enumerate details of construction not essential to the invention, and the Claim cannot be limited to these details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ex parte Laskey (1889). Claims identify essentials; descriptions supply nonessential detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature not in Description cannot be claimed despite drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: That a feature not alluded to in the Description cannot be covered by the Claim, though it appears in the drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Gunn v. Savage (1887). Description requirement for claimed features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressions adjacent to Claim can be part of Claim
rubrics_metrics.description: That any perfectly clear expression of what the inventor intends to secure to himself in immediate connection with the Claim is virtually part of the Claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: La Rue v. Western Electric Co. (1886). Surrounding language may inform claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: File-wrapper may interpret the Claim
rubrics_metrics.description: That the file-wrapper and contents may interpret the Claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Royer v. Coupe (1889). Prosecution history is relevant to claim interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement-only inventor cannot claim entire means
rubrics_metrics.description: That the inventor of an improvement only cannot claim the entire means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ex parte Miller (1888). Limitations on improvement inventors' scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims restricted by PTO not deprived of equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: That a patentee who has accepted a patent with Claims restricted by the Patent Office is not limited to the letter of his Claims, nor deprived of the right to equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Consolidated Roller-Mill Co. v. Coombs (1889). Doctrine of equivalents survives prosecution restriction.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'As shown and described' implied in Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: That 'as shown and described' will be implied by the courts in all Claims, but is usually required by the Patent Office, especially in design patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ex parte Gerard (1888). Standard phrasing interpreting claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain generic words sometimes proper in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: That the words 'means,' 'mechanism,' 'connections,' are sometimes proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ex parte Stoughton (1888); Ex parte Stanbridge (1888). Functional language may be allowable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination vs aggregation: new result test
rubrics_metrics.description: That the effecting a new result as distinguished from an aggregation of old results is one test of a combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Shipman Engine Co. v. Rochester Tool Works (1888). Patentable combination must produce a new cooperative result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grouping without new result is aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: That where no result is attained by grouping elements beyond their separate or collective result, the grouping is an aggregation, not a combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Richards v. Michigan Cent. R.R. Co. (1889). Mere juxtaposition isn't patentable combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements must co-act for combination patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: That where the elements do not co-act to produce a new result, there is no patentable combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Brinkerhoff v. Aloe (1888). Functional interaction is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination must perform beyond sum of separate functions
rubrics_metrics.description: That a combination must perform a function beyond that which is the sum of the functions of its separated elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ide v. Ball Engine Co. (1889); Jones v. Glow (1889). Synergistic effect required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series of identical devices not a combination
rubrics_metrics.description: That a series of identical devices is not a combination, but each device is a complete thing by itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Morrison v. Ganton Surgical and Dental Chair Co. (1889). Repetition of units doesn't create a combination claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of one element from combination not new invention
rubrics_metrics.description: That the omission from a patented combination of one element, leaving the other elements to co-act just as they did before, is not a new invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: McClain v. Ortmayer (1887). Removing nonessential element doesn't create a new patentable combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: All claimed elements are essential in a combination claim
rubrics_metrics.description: That all claimed elements of a combination are thereby made essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Thompson v. Gildersleeve (1888). Claim drafting must account for essentiality of recited elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner duties partly ministerial partly judicial
rubrics_metrics.description: That the duties of the Commissioner are partly ministerial, partly judicial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Daniel v. Morgan (1889). Nature of PTO/Commissioner functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner lacks jurisdiction over title conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: That the Commissioner has no jurisdiction over conflicts as to title, nor can he recognize equitable or contract rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: McDonough v. Gray (1889). Equitable disputes not for administrative resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception proven by description only when detailed
rubrics_metrics.description: That conception is proved by description only when the description shows that the conceiver had not merely perceived the desirability of a result, but the way and means of effecting it, so that a listener to the description, if skilled in the art, could produce it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Wherry v. Heck (1889). Conception requires enabling descriptive disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings/models higher evidence of conception than oral descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: That drawings and models are much higher evidence of conception than oral descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Wherry v. Heck (1889). Prefer tangible evidence of conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandoned application may evidence conception
rubrics_metrics.description: That an abandoned application may show conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Beach v. Fowler (1889). Earlier filings can be evidence of earlier conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents construed in light of common knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: That patents are to be construed in the light of common knowledge as to what was in use before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Formcrook Mfg. Co. v. Iron Works (1886). Claim interpretation includes prior art context known to skilled artisans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construal to protect actual invention if language permits
rubrics_metrics.description: That a patent is to be construed in view of the state of the art and so as to protect the actual invention, if its language will permit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Consolidated Roller Mill Co. v. Coombs (1889). Give claims reasonable scope to cover the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent cannot be construed to cover parts not described or claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: That a patent cannot be construed to cover parts not described or claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ball & Socket Fastener Co. v. Kraetzer (1889). Construction cannot expand to undescribed matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow claim enlargement only by reissue
rubrics_metrics.description: That a narrow Claim must be enlarged by re-issue, if at all, not by construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Becker v. Hastings (1884). Reissue procedure required to broaden claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot retroactively give new construction not contemplated at drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: That a construction not contemplated when the Claim was drawn cannot be afterwards given to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ladd v. Mooney (1884). Limits on post-hoc reinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim defines PTO-determined scope; cannot be enlarged by construction
rubrics_metrics.description: That the claim of a patent defines what the Patent Office has determined to be the scope of the invention, and it cannot be enlarged by construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Day v. Fair Haven & Westville R.R. Co. (1889); U.S. Supreme Court references. Claim scope set by PTO determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: After claim modification to meet PTO, cannot enlarge by construction
rubrics_metrics.description: That after the Claim has been modified in obedience to the Patent Office it cannot be enlarged by construction to cover the relinquished matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Phoenix Caster Co. v. Spiegel (1890); Roemer v. Peddie (1889). Prosecution concessions binding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts may examine file-wrapper in construing claims
rubrics_metrics.description: That the court in construing the Claims may examine the file-wrapper and contents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Consolidated Roller-Mill Co. v. Coombs (1889). Prosecution history is admissible to clarify meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction by PTO in allowing claim will be followed
rubrics_metrics.description: That the construction put upon a Claim by the Patent Office in allowing it, as shown by the correspondence, will be followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Royer v. Schultz Belting Co. (1889). Deference to PTO's allowance construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear claim obviates need to consult drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: That where the Claim is clear the drawings need not be considered in construing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Bidd v. Horry (1888). Primary weight to clear claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express or implied contract may govern use of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: That the right to use a patented invention may be the subject of a contract express or implied, and assumpsit will lie to recover reasonable compensation for its use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Deane v. Hodge (1886). Contracts can create enforceable rights to use patented inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied contract damages = reasonable royalty
rubrics_metrics.description: That under an implied contract for the use of an invention the measure of recovery is a reasonable royalty, as custom or expert evidence as to utility and value may indicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Deane v. Hodge (1886). Damages for implied license measured by royalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents can be partnership capital contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: That patents may be contributed to the capital of a partnership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Rehfus v. Moore (1889). Patents treated as partnership assets when contributed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of half-interest and joint exploitation creates partnership
rubrics_metrics.description: That where a patentee assigns a half-interest in the patent to a capitalist, and they unite in making and selling the invention, they are partners, and at the death of one the business should be wound up and proceeds divided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Farr v. Morrill (1889). Business relationships from assignment plus joint activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warranty scope vs different machine sales
rubrics_metrics.description: That a warranty guaranteeing the exclusive sale of one machine within certain territory is not broken by the sale of a different machine in the same territory under the same patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Pratt v. Marean (1888). Warranty interpretation focuses on the machine specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of license on royalties implies agreement to pay
rubrics_metrics.description: That the acceptance of a license on condition of royalties is an agreement to pay the royalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Paper Stock Disinfecting Co. v. Boston Disinfecting Co. (1888). Consent to license terms creates payment obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee liable for stipulated royalty even if using subset of inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: That a licensee under a patent covering several inventions is liable for the stipulated royalty, whether he uses one or all of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Hubbard v. Allen (1889). Broad license terms enforceable as written.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreements regulating mutual enjoyment of patent rights not restraint of trade
rubrics_metrics.description: That a contract regulating the mutual enjoyment of patent-rights is not 'in restraint of trade.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Bowling v. Taylor (1889). Antitrust considerations distinct from patent license arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overly broad restrictions in transfers may be void
rubrics_metrics.description: That a restriction in a transfer of rights under a patent being greater than is reasonably necessary to protect the purchaser is void as against public policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Berlin Mach. Works v. Perry (1888). Public policy limits on restrictive covenants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to procure patent may void assignment obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: That an agreement to procure and assign a patent fails if the patent is not procured or procurable, and the purchase money may be recovered by the promisee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Westerfelt v. Fuller Mfg. Co. (1885). Remedies for failed procurement promises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity may compel assignment to equitable owners
rubrics_metrics.description: That equity may compel the assignment of a patent by the legal owner to those equitably entitled to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Berolzheimer v. Strauss (1884). Specific equitable remedies for ownership disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: State courts may compel specific performance of assignment/license contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: That State courts of equity will compel specific performance of contracts for assignment or license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Fuller & Johnson Mfg. Co. v. Bartlett (1887). Specific performance applicable to patent deals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parol/Oral agreements to assign or license may be enforced
rubrics_metrics.description: That a parol agreement to assign a patent may be enforced in equity, and the court may direct execution of necessary papers; an oral contract for a license to use an invention may be enforced in equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Searle v. Hill (1887); Nichols v. Marsh (1886). Oral promises can warrant equitable relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement to apply and assign foreign patents enforceable
rubrics_metrics.description: That an agreement to apply for and assign foreign patents will be enforced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Adams v. Messinger (1888). International prosecution obligations may be contractually enforceable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement to make/deliver patented article enforceable when no special skill required
rubrics_metrics.description: That an agreement by the owner of a patent to make and deliver the patented article will be enforced in equity, where no special skill is required to make it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Adams v. Messinger (1888). Practical manufacturing contracts enforceable by equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific performance not decreed where defendant lacks title or patent void
rubrics_metrics.description: That specific performance of an agreement to convey a patent will not be decreed where the defendant has no title or the patent is void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Kennedy v. Hazelton (1888). Equitable relief contingent on existence of title and valid patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific performance of old patent not decreed
rubrics_metrics.description: That the specific performance of an old patent will not be decreed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Kennedy v. Hazelton (1888). Time/validity factors affect equitable remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconscionable contracts not enforced in equity
rubrics_metrics.description: That an unconscionable contract will not be enforced in equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Pope Mfg. Co. v. Gormully (1888). Equity refuses relief against unfair terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Owner may be enjoined against alienating or encumbering patent title
rubrics_metrics.description: That the owner of a patent may be enjoined against alienating or encumbering his title thereto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Adams v. Messinger (1888). Court can preserve equitable title by injunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract to purchase obtained by fraud rescindable
rubrics_metrics.description: That a contract to purchase a patent right obtained by the fraud of the vendor will be rescinded in equity, and the parties placed in status quo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Marsh v. Scott (1888). Fraud vitiates transfer agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election required between rescission and affirmance
rubrics_metrics.description: That a party having the right to a rescission and an affirmance of a contract must make his election and abide by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Creighton v. Haggerty (1884). Procedural posture for remedy choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages must be proved, not conjectured
rubrics_metrics.description: That damages must be proved, not conjectured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Rude v. Westcott (1889). Burden of proof for monetary relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: License fees paid voluntarily are evidence of established fee
rubrics_metrics.description: That license fees fixed by plaintiff and voluntarily paid by licensees, are evidence of an established fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: United Nickel Co. v. Central Pac. R. Co. (1888). Licenses as evidence of market value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Established license fee requires frequent occurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: That a license fee is established only where the payment of such fees is of frequent occurrence and shows the value of the license in similar cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Rude v. Westcott (1889). Single or rare payments may be insufficient proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two instances may show established license fee
rubrics_metrics.description: That two instances are admissible to show an established license fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Cary v. Lovell Mfg. Co. (1889). Minimal repeated transactions can support proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irregular/uncertain rates do not show license fee
rubrics_metrics.description: That irregular and uncertain rates for licenses do not show a license fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: United Nickel Co. v. Central Pac. R. Co. (1888). Consistency required for reliable evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular license fee not varied by occasional departures
rubrics_metrics.description: That when a regular license fee exists it is not varied by occasional departures in cases of necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Assmus v. Freeman (1888). Outliers don't change established licensing practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court allowance per article doesn't fix royalty/right to interest
rubrics_metrics.description: That an allowance of a sum per article by a court as damages does not fix a royalty or give a right to interest thereon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Graham v. Piano Mfg. Co. (1888). Damages formulation distinct from licensing terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement payment not measure of invention value
rubrics_metrics.description: That the payment of a sum in settlement of an infringement does not measure the value of the invention or the damages sustained in other cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Rude v. Westcott (1889); Comely v. Harckwald (1889). Private settlement amounts not determinative of general damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty for one right not evidence for different right's damages
rubrics_metrics.description: That a royalty paid for one right under a patent, or for all the rights, is not evidence of damages for infringing a single different right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Colgate v. Western Electric Mfg. Co. (1886). Allocation of royalties to specific rights matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty for several patents jointly not evidence for each
rubrics_metrics.description: That a royalty paid for several patents jointly does not show the license fee for either.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Vulcanite Paving Co. v. American Artificial Pavement Co. (1888). Bundled licensing complicates valuation of individual patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss of profits measure when no license fee exists
rubrics_metrics.description: That where there is no license fee the measure of damages is the profits lost by the patentee by reason of the infringement, and he must show to what extent sales have been diverted from him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Covert v. Sargent (1889). Proof of diversion and lost sales required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of damages when plaintiff does not grant licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: That where the plaintiff does not grant licenses, the measure of damages for an infringing sale is the amount of profit he would have made if he had sold what the defendant sold, deducting a fair percentage in respect of sales due to the particular exertions of the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: United Horse Shoe & Nail Co. v. Stewart (1888). Account for defendant's contribution to sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstantial evidence may show lost sales
rubrics_metrics.description: That the plaintiff may show by circumstantial as well as direct evidence that he would have sold the articles sold by the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Covert v. Sargent (1889). Use indirect proof when direct evidence lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior purchases by defendant create presumption of diversion
rubrics_metrics.description: That where defendants, before infringing, bought of the plaintiff, as also during the infringement to some extent, it is a fair presumption that they would have bought of him all they made and used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Creamer v. Bowers (1888). Past purchasing patterns support lost-sales claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff must show extent price reduction due to infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: That a plaintiff who claims a loss by reduction of prices must show by sufficient data to what extent such reduction was due to the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Boesch v. Grff (1890); Comely v. Harckwald (1889). Causation required for price-related damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of lost contracts inadmissible if plaintiff priced same with/without invention
rubrics_metrics.description: That when the plaintiff charged no more when he used his invention than when he did not use it, evidence that he lost valuable contracts through the defendant's competition is inadmissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Vulcanite Paving Co. v. American Artificial Stone Pavement Co. (1888). Damages must be tied to economic effect of invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flagrant injury may lead to treble damages
rubrics_metrics.description: That for a flagrant injury damages will be trebled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Lyon v. Donaldson (1888). Exemplary damages available for willful/wanton misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair, bona fide contests not basis for increased damages
rubrics_metrics.description: That a strenuous contest, if fair and bona fide, is no reason for increasing the damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Welling v. La Ban (1888). Litigation conduct alone not sufficient for punitive increase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court will not increase damages merely for defendant soliciting customers
rubrics_metrics.description: That a court will not increase the damages merely because the defendant urged his goods on the plaintiff's customers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Morss v. Union Form Co. (1889). Competitive solicitation not automatically aggravating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may award damages in equity then treble them
rubrics_metrics.description: That the court may award damages in equity in excess of the profits and then treble them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Tilghman v. Proctor (1888). Equity may fashion larger relief including trebled amounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may refuse to increase damages based on omitted evidence of invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: That while after final decree the defendant may not be allowed to offer evidence, before carelessly omitted, to show that the patent is void, yet in view thereof the court may refuse to increase the damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Welling v. La Ban (1888). Patent validity issues may limit damage enhancements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer of nominal damages can bind plaintiff without compromise
rubrics_metrics.description: That a plaintiff, not having any compromise in view, is bound by an offer to accept nominal damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Creamer v. Bowers (1888). Offers can limit plaintiff's recovery when accepted or unchallenged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest allowed on royalties but not on unliquidated damages
rubrics_metrics.description: That interest is allowed on royalties, but not on unliquidated damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Creamer v. Bowers (1888). Distinguish liquidated (royalty) vs unliquidated sums for interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign patentee cannot claim earlier invention date than foreign patent
rubrics_metrics.description: That a foreign patentee cannot claim an earlier date for his invention than that of his foreign patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Electrical Accumulator Co. v. Julien Electric Co. (1889). Priority tied to foreign filing dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic statement of foreign patent not proof of its existence
rubrics_metrics.description: That a statement in the domestic specification that the applicant has obtained a foreign patent does not prove that fact nor carry back the prima facie date of his invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Electrical Accumulator Co. v. Julien Electric Co. (1889). Self-serving statements insufficient to establish earlier priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: American patent date need not match foreign patent date limiting its term
rubrics_metrics.description: That the date of the American patent need not correspond with that of the foreign one by which its term is limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: The Telephone Cases (1888). Term limitations based on foreign filings operate independently of domestic issue dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each application must be complete in itself
rubrics_metrics.description: That one pending application cannot refer to another for a fuller description, but each must be complete in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ex parte Borgfeldt (1889); Ex parte Everitt (1889). Self-contained sufficiency required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inaccurate statements about good results don't render Description defective
rubrics_metrics.description: That inaccurate statements concerning the good results of a patented process do not render the Description defective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Michaelis v. Roesaler (1888). Puffery about results not necessarily enabling-sufficiency issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraudulent concealment requires intent to deceive
rubrics_metrics.description: That the defence of fraudulent concealment is not supported unless an intent to deceive is shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Celluloid Mfg. Co. v. Russell (1889). Mens rea required for fraud-based defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description addressed to skilled in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: That the Description is addressed to those skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Celluloid Mfg. Co. v. Russell (1889). Enablement judged by those of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific invention Description addressed to learned in science
rubrics_metrics.description: That the Description of a scientific invention is addressed to those learned in the science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Electrical Accumulator Co. v. Julien Electric Co. (1889). Technical sophistication expected for scientific subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process Description must be intelligible and practical for skilled artisans
rubrics_metrics.description: That the Description of a process must describe it in a manner intelligible to those skilled in the art, and point out a way to make it practical, but it is not required that it be brought to the highest degree of perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: The Telephone Cases (1888). Enablement requires practical, not perfect, instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification sufficient if skilled mechanic can construct
rubrics_metrics.description: That the Description is sufficient if a skilled mechanic could from it construct the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Pullman Palace Car Co. v. Wagner Palace Car Co. (1889). Functional standard for enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical specification sufficiency judged by chemists
rubrics_metrics.description: That the specification of a chemical patent is addressed to those skilled in chemistry and is sufficient if intelligible to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Am Ende v. Seabury (1888); Anilin v. Levinstein (1887). Technical audience standard for chemical patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patentable if new appearance creates demand
rubrics_metrics.description: That a design presenting a new appearance to the eye, and creating a demand for the goods on which it is impressed, is patentable though simple and resembling other designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Untermyer v. Freund (1889). Commercial distinctiveness and visual novelty matter for designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design novelty judged by ordinary observers
rubrics_metrics.description: That a design is not new unless it would appear to ordinary observers to be different from the old, but the difference may be small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Redway v. Ohio Stove Co. (1889). Objective observer standard for design identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of old designs may be patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: That a patent for a combination of old designs is proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Whitman Saddle Co. v. Smith (1889). Assemblies of existing designs can be protectable if presentation novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every design is finished and distinct entity
rubrics_metrics.description: That every design is a finished and distinct entity, not a combination, nor a genus, nor a species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ex parte Gerard (1888). Treat designs as discrete units for protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design may also constitute a manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: That a design may be also a manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ex parte Gerard (1888). Overlap between design and manufacture categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of designs measured by appearance to ordinary observers
rubrics_metrics.description: That the identity of designs is measured by their appearance to ordinary observers, not to experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Redway v. Ohio Stove Co. (1889); Ex parte Gerard (1888); Kraus v. Fitzpatrick (1888). Lay perception controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer statutes treated as single law with same conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: That ss. 4917 and 4922 Rev. Stat. concerning disclaimers are parts of one law and require the same conditions for amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Hailes v. Albany Stove Co. (1887). Statutory interpretation of disclaimer provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer cannot change character of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: That a disclaimer cannot change the character of the patented invention nor render further description necessary, but can only eliminate separable matter from the Claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Hailes v. Albany Stove Co. (1887). Disclaimers strictly limit claims; they don't alter invention nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer cannot convert apparatus patent into process patent
rubrics_metrics.description: That a patent for the apparatus cannot be changed into one for the process by disclaiming the apparatus except when used in the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Grant v. Walter (1889). Disclaimers cannot shift statutory category except in narrow circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer affects Claims, not Description
rubrics_metrics.description: That a disclaimer is not needed when the Description is excessive but not the Claim — the Claim controlling the Description and limiting the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Brush Electric Co. v. Fort Wayne Electric Light Co. (1889). Claims control patent scope; disclaimers operate on claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer of separable excess may save valid portion of Claim
rubrics_metrics.description: That a disclaimer of the separable excess may save the valid portion of the Claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Electrical Accumulator Co. v. Julien Electric Co. (1889). Strategic disclaimers can preserve patentable core.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee bound by claim narrowed to meet PTO objection
rubrics_metrics.description: That the patentee is bound by a Claim which has been narrowed to meet an unfounded objection in the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Lapham Dodge Co. v. Severin (1889). Prosecution concessions generally binding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delayed disclaimer to save suit not permissible after unreasonable delay
rubrics_metrics.description: That a disclaimer to save an otherwise lost suit is not permissible after unreasonable delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Hake v. Brown (1889). Timeliness required for post-litigation disclaimers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer admissible after merits only on rehearing and terms
rubrics_metrics.description: That a disclaimer cannot be put in evidence after decision on the merits in equity, except upon a rehearing and on such terms as the court may impose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Roemer v. Bernheim (1889). Post-decision disclaimers tightly constrained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventions by hired inventors equitably belong to employer
rubrics_metrics.description: That the inventions of a person hired to invent, and to patent his inventions in the name of the employer, equitably belong to the employer, and if patented to the inventor he may be compelled in equity to assign his patent to the employer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Annin v. Wren (1887). Employment agreements and equitable assignment principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer may patent employees' inventions with consent
rubrics_metrics.description: That an employer may patent the inventions of his employees for his own benefit if they consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Dueber Watch-Case Mfg. Co. v. Dalzell (1889). Consent shapes ownership rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee disclosure/use licenses employer but does not transfer future patent rights
rubrics_metrics.description: That an employee disclosing his invention to the employer, and putting it to practical use in the employment, does not thereby transfer a right to the invention itself and the future patent therefor, but licenses the employer to use it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Fuller & Johnson Mfg. Co. v. Bartlett (1887). Use in employment confers license, not automatic assignment absent agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devices may be equivalents though one better than other
rubrics_metrics.description: That devices may be equivalents though one answers the purpose better than the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Roosevelt v. Law Tel. Co. (1887). Equivalence assessed by functional interchangeability, not relative superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known equivalent defined
rubrics_metrics.description: That a 'known equivalent' is such a substitute as is known to be able to accomplish the same result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Morley Mach. Co. v. Lancaster (1889). Prior knowledge of substitutability is relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalents may be recognized even if knowledge arose after invention
rubrics_metrics.description: That equivalents are such though it could not have been known that they would be equivalents until after the device in which they are employed was invented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Morley Mach. Co. v. Lancaster (1889). Temporal knowledge does not necessarily preclude equivalents doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee entitled to equivalents despite claim reforms
rubrics_metrics.description: That a patentee is entitled to equivalents though he may have reformed his Claims under requirements of the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Rodebaugh v. Jackson (1889). Prosecution amendments do not forfeit equivalents entitlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney in fact not estopped to deny validity when conveying under power
rubrics_metrics.description: That an attorney in fact, conveying the patent under a power, is not estopped to deny validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: H. Tibbe & Son Mfg. Co. v. Heineker (1889). Power-of-attorney conveyances do not necessarily bind attorney's substantive positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement vs original not always species-genus relation
rubrics_metrics.description: That the relation of an improvement to its original is not always that of species to a genus — a species being created only when an original generic element is supplanted by a new or modified element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ex parte Smith (1888). Taxonomic analogies depend on substantive replacement of generic elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process and its apparatus distinct inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: That a process and its apparatus are not genus and species but distinct inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Ex parte Atwood (1888). Distinguish statutory categories when evaluating claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater perfection does not show lack of identity
rubrics_metrics.description: That greater perfection in the result effected does not show want of identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: MacDonald v. McLean (1889). Improvements that improve but do not change identity still relate to original invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of invention for different purpose is infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: That use of the invention for a different purpose is infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Thompson v. Gildersleeve (1888). Purpose-based use does not immunize infringing use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of part to those with right to use is not infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: That the sale of part of an invention to those who have a right to use it is not an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Morgan Envelope Co. v. Albany Perforated Wrapping Paper Co. (1889). Authorized recipients/sales can be noninfringing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of element with innocent uses not infringement absent collusion
rubrics_metrics.description: That the sale of an element capable of an innocent use, and without collusion, does not infringe the patent for the combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Winne v. Bedell (1889). Component sales with substantial noninfringing uses protected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint infringement is one tort; recovery bars further proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: That a joint infringement is one tort, and recovery of satisfaction against one tort-feasor is a bar to further proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Babcock & Wilcox Co. v. Pioneer Iron Works (1888). Release/settlement implications in multi-defendant contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate acts by different parties with common purpose can infringe
rubrics_metrics.description: That a patent may be infringed by the separate acts of different parties having a common purpose, though no one act is by itself an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Celluloid Mfg. Co. v. American Zylonite Co. (1887). Concerted division-of-step infringement recognized.

rubrics_metrics.name: United ownership of conflicting patents treats one as improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: That when the titles to two conflicting patents are united in one owner, one invention may be treated as an improvement on the other as against an infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Putnam v. Keystone Bottle Stopper Co. (1889). Consolidation of rights affects enforcement posture.

rubrics_metrics.name: User under both patents may be liable for each patent's uncovered use
rubrics_metrics.description: That where two patents cover in part the same field, a party who has used under both may be held liable for that in each which was not covered by the other, and cannot claim that the later was void because anticipated by the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Deane v. Hodge (1886). Coexistence of multiple patent rights can lead to separate liabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination patent infringed if substance taken despite equivalents/alterations
rubrics_metrics.description: That a combination-patent is infringed if the substance of the combination is taken, whatever equivalents, alterations, or omissions may be resorted to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Proctor v. Bennis (1887). Substantial appropriation standard for combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination not infringed unless all elements or equivalents used
rubrics_metrics.description: That a combination is not infringed unless all its elements or their equivalents are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Perkins v. Eaton (1889). Complete practice of a combination or equivalents required for infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taking some elements with equivalents infringes combination
rubrics_metrics.description: That taking some of the elements with equivalents for the others infringes the combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Leary v. Hohenstein (1889). Mixed literal/equivalent element practice can infringe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstruction after patent expiration not infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: That the reconstruction of a combination after its patent has expired is not an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Johnson v. Brooklyn & C.R. Co. (1888). Post-expiration recreations are in the public domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art patent not infringed if some steps omitted
rubrics_metrics.description: That a patent for an art is not infringed if some of its steps are omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Royer v. Coupe (1889). Process infringement requires practice of claimed essential steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process infringed by employing essence regardless of apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: That a process is infringed by employing the essence of the invention, whatever apparatus may be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Morley Mach. Co. v. Lancaster (1889). Substance-over-form approach to process infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine patent infringed by different mechanism performing same means/results
rubrics_metrics.description: That a machine performing new functions is infringed by any mechanism which employs the same means to accomplish the same results, though its parts are individually improved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Morley Mach. Co. v. Lancaster (1889). Functional equivalence can infringe machine patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design may infringe despite infringer's name coupling
rubrics_metrics.description: That a design may infringe though the infringer's name be coupled with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Redway v. Ohio Stove Co. (1889). Labeling/credit doesn't avoid design infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government use measured by implied contract absent special agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: That in the absence of any special agreement the acts of the government in using an invention measure its liability under an implied contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Butler v. United States (1888). Sovereign use creates compensation obligations akin to implied license.
